newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Buba continues assault against euro one-offs.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Buba continues assault against euro one-offs.

text.p: Two more board members of the German Bundesbank on Tuesday warned against taking "one-off" measures to fulfil economic criteria for Europe's monetary union (EMU), saying long-term stability was more important.

While Edgar Meister did not specifically refer to Bonn's plan to revalue central bank reserves in his call for lasting convergence measures, board colleague Reimut Jochimsen renewed his outspoken attack on the scheme in a newspaper interview.

Since the Bundesbank declared its opposition to the gold and currency revaluation plan late last Wednesday, seven of its senior officials have spoken out against Bonn's move to use its reserves in the push towards EMU.

"Many European countries are facing problems in taking the three percent hurdle, even if one does not insist that it be met exactly," Meister said in the text of a speech to be delivered to a conference in Kaernten, Austria, on Tuesday.

European countries are required to cut their budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product this year if they want to join the euro at its planned launch in 1999, with Germany traditionally supporting a strict interpretation of such measures.

"In Germany (however), prospects for budget developments are now less favourable than was assumed a few months ago," Meister warned, adding that this meant there could be no abandonment of consolidation measures.
"It would be more important to take measures which will have a long-term effect than to achieve an exact fulfilment which is only achieved through one-off measures," he said.

Meister said long-term convergence would moreover be important for the lasting success of the euro and that the so-called stability pact, a mechanism designed to ensure this stability after monetary union, would be the key.

Jochimsen, who on Friday warned of the "disastrous" consequences of Bonn's reserves revaluation plan, continued his campaign in a newspaper interview on Tuesday, saying such actions put the qualification process this year at risk.

"The year 1997 is decisive for measuring suitability (for participation in the project). This process must not be messed up by one-off measures," Jochimsen said in the Westdeutsche Allgemeine Zeitung.
He added that the economic criteria for entry must be fulfilled "honestly and sustainably" and that the government's gold scheme did not match up to this requirement.
